title: Route plugin settings through Settings as a namespaced overlay (Option A)
wave: 7 of 8 (M2) — alongside WI-8b and WI-9; depends on nothing, deliberately held here per §5.1 C
one_line: Plugin settings stop living in two side-channel JSON files and start living inside the existing Settings layers under a reserved `plugins.<id>.<key>` namespace, so a plugin setting gets the same six-layer tiering (runtime → overlay → project → global → parent → default, plus env) that core settings already get, and `provenance()` can name which layer won.
user_visible_effect: Plugin settings become editable in the normal settings panel with a visible source layer, and can be overridden by an environment variable the plugin declares. Nothing changes for a user who never touches a plugin setting: existing values are migrated silently, in place, with no prompt and no re-auth.
one_line_why_this_is_the_whole_job: Option A changes the SUBSTRATE, not the API. `getPluginSettings` / `setPluginSetting` / `deletePluginSetting` keep their signatures; what changes is which store answers them. Namespacing is the load-bearing half, not the plumbing half, because `register()` throws on a duplicate id — an unnamespaced plugin key that collides with a core id breaks at plugin LOAD time rather than degrading.

files_touched.change: Add the namespace primitives: `pluginSettingId(pluginId, key)`, `sanitizePluginSegment(raw)`, and an idempotent `registerPluginSetting(definition)` that looks the id up before calling `register()`. This is where a plugin's `manifest.settings` schema becomes typed handles.

No `all-settings.ts` edit is needed — which also means this file does NOT touch blocker 1 of WI-8b, so 8b stays unblocked.

files_touched.change: Rewrite `getPluginSettings` (929), `setPluginSetting` (942) and `deletePluginSetting` (954) to read/write through registered `plugins.*` handles on the Settings instance, and add a one-time idempotent migration that folds BOTH legacy files into the new shape.

The plan did NOT mention that they must be retained for the migration even though they are exactly the store being replaced — deleting them is how the data-loss bug the plan warns about actually happens.

files_touched.change: Make the module-level `getPluginSettings(pluginName, cwd)` (474) delegate to the new substrate instead of re-implementing the merge against the two legacy files.

It is a byte-for-byte second copy of the `{ ...global, ...project }` merge, it is re-exported through the `extensibility/plugins` barrel, and it is the read path an extension calls by name. Migrating only `manager.ts` leaves the extension-facing surface reading the legacy files forever — a second instance of the exact 'two read paths, you migrate one' bug the plan calls out as the main hazard. Verified no in-repo caller, which is precisely why it would have been missed: its consumer is third-party code.

The `PluginManager` side uses the `spyOn(piUtils, ...)` pattern already proven in `test/plugin-config.test.ts:25-33`. No `mock.module()` anywhere.

steps.instruction: Write the namespace primitives into `extensibility/settings.ts`: `sanitizePluginSegment`, `PLUGIN_SETTINGS_ROOT`, `pluginSettingId`, and `registerPluginSetting`. The idempotency in step 1 is NOT optional polish — it is the difference between this item and a landmine for WI-7 and WI-9. Before writing it, confirm the registry is append-only yourself: grep `byId` and `ordered` in `config/registry.ts` and observe that `byId.set` (:789) and `ordered.push` (:790) are the only mutations, and that `resetRegistryForTest` (:953) touches only the `effects` array, never `byId`/`ordered`. Add the `lookup` import from `../config/registry` alongside the existing `combine`/`register` import.

Build the schema→definition adapter. Each plugin declares its settings in its manifest as `PluginSettingSchema` (`extensibility/plugins/types.ts:48` — `settings?: Record<string, PluginSettingSchema>`), which is a looser shape than `SettingDefinition` (it carries `type`, `default`, `description`, `secret`, `options`). Map it: `default` carries over, `description` becomes `ui.description`, `secret` becomes `ui.secret`, `options` becomes `ui.options`, and `type` maps onto the registry's type vocabulary — read the accepted `type` strings off `SettingDefinition` in `config/registry.ts` rather than guessing. Read the manifest through the EXISTING accessor (`manager.ts:256`, and the two other read sites at `:622` and `:845`) — do not open a fourth path to the manifest.

Decide and write down the env-variable naming rule BEFORE you write the test, in the same commit: `OMP_<PLUGIN_ID>_<KEY>`, uppercase, `-` and `.` folded to `_`, spelled out literally in `SettingDefinition.env` by the plugin. No variable name is ever synthesised from an id. Note the asymmetry that makes this opt-in and therefore testable: a plugin that declares no `env` does not join the sixth layer at all, because `envValue()` bails at `config/registry.ts:515` when `!this.envName`. A test row asserting `"env"` for a key with no declared `env` must FAIL — that is the correct behaviour, not a bug to paper over.

Rewrite `setPluginSetting` FIRST — this is the write path and it must land before any read path changes. Route it through `handle.set(scope, value)`, which writes the global layer at `config/settings.ts:828` and queues the debounced save. Confirm the old side-channel write is gone: `setPluginSetting` must no longer call `#saveRuntimeConfig`. Do NOT delete `#saveRuntimeConfig` or `#loadProjectOverrides` yet — step 6 still needs them.

Rewrite `getPluginSettings` and `deletePluginSetting` to go through the same registered handles. `deletePluginSetting` becomes `handle.unset(scope)` → `unsetGlobalValue` (`config/settings.ts:845`), which deletes from the GLOBAL layer only and lets a project-layer value resurface. Flag this: the old behaviour deleted the key outright. Raise it (see open_questions) rather than silently shipping the change.

Add the one-time migration, and get its shape right — it is the whole data-loss risk of this item. It MUST read BOTH legacy shapes, because `setPluginSetting` has never once written to the second file: (a) `settings[name]` in the runtime config written by `#saveRuntimeConfig` → `~/.omp/omp-plugins.lock.json` (path from `getPluginsLockfile`, `utils/src/dirs.ts:652`), and (b) `settings?.[name]` in `<project>/.omp/plugin-overrides.json` (`ProjectPluginOverrides`, `extensibility/plugins/types.ts:156`; path from `getProjectPluginOverridesPath`, `utils/src/dirs.ts:1046`), read via `#loadProjectOverrides` (`manager.ts:153`). Merge with project winning — that is the current `{ ...global, ...project }` order — then write into the `plugins.*` handles via `set()`. Guard it with a persisted completion marker.

The completion marker is not bookkeeping, it is a correctness requirement. Without it the migration re-runs on every start and RESURRECTS a key the user deliberately deleted after the first migration — a value deleted in the new store is still sitting in the legacy file, so a re-run silently brings it back. The marker must be written only AFTER the new shape is durably persisted, and it must be namespaced to this migration so a future substrate change can migrate again deliberately. Verify the marker's own write path is the Settings layer or a dedicated marker file — never a third plugin store, or this item has recreated the problem it was written to remove.

Make `loader.ts`'s module-level `getPluginSettings(pluginName, cwd)` (474) delegate to the new substrate. This function is a byte-for-byte second copy of the merge logic, it is re-exported through the `extensibility/plugins` barrel, and it is the function an extension calls by name. Leaving it on the legacy files means the extension-facing surface never migrates. The plan does not mention this file at all — it is the single most likely way to ship this item half-done, because `git grep` finds no in-repo caller and the code looks dead.

Leave the Plugins tab and the TUI overlay alone. `settings-selector.ts:438` (NOT :435 — see plan_corrections) hard-codes `{ id: "plugins", label: ... }` and the read path `tui/src/overlays/plugin-settings.ts:147` goes through the unchanged `PluginSettingsHost` interface declared at `:71`. Merging plugin settings into the main settings panel is WI-8b blocker 4, explicitly out of scope here. Confirm by reading that `PluginSettingsManager` (`:71`) still type-checks unchanged — if the host interface had to change, this item has leaked into 8b.

Write `test/config/plugin-settings-provenance.test.ts` — three groups, in the order below, because the order encodes the data-loss contract. Row 1 and row 2 are the migration rows; row 3 is the tiering row. See test_contract for the exact assertions.

Run the gate. `bun test` is BLOCKED in this environment until the native addon is built — the harness reported this and I reproduced it: `0 pass, 1 fail` with `Cannot find module .../pi_natives.darwin-arm64.node`. Build first with `bun --cwd=packages/natives run build`, then run the test. `bun run check:ts` needs no addon and I confirmed it is GREEN on HEAD right now, so it is a usable gate today.

Add the changelog line under `## [Unreleased]` → `### Changed` in `packages/coding-agent/CHANGELOG.md`. One line, user-facing, no root-cause narration: lead with what the user can now do (plugin settings live in the main settings file and honour a declared environment variable).

test_contract.the_contract: A namespaced plugin setting participates in the SAME six-layer tiering as a core setting: a project-layer value is overridden by the environment variable the plugin declared, and `Setting.provenance(scope)` NAMES the layer that won.
test_contract.how_it_fails_observably: On the substrate this replaces, the env override is silently ignored for plugin keys and nothing can report which source won, because the side-channel store has no layer to name. A user sets `OMP_GRAPHIFY_AUTO_CONTEXT_ENABLED=1`, the plugin still reads the project file's `false`, and neither the plugin nor the UI can say why. This is invisible until a user actually has a plugin setting configured — which is exactly why it survived five review rounds.
test_contract.assert_through: `Setting.provenance(scope)` at `config/registry.ts:764-765`, NEVER `Settings.getProvenance` (`config/settings.ts:800-808`). The latter checks runtime → overlay → project → global → parent → default and can never return `"env"`, even though `"env"` is in the `SettingProvenance` union at `settings.ts:62`. Asserting through the wrong surface would pass while the contract is broken.
test_contract.assert_both: BOTH the resolved value AND the reported layer. Asserting the value alone passes on a store that happens to read the right file — which is precisely the accidental-pass the plan warns about.
test_contract.fails_on_head_today: Yes. On HEAD `getPluginSettings` returns `{ ...global, ...project }` with no env step at all, and the `Setting.provenance(scope)` surface does not exist for a plugin key because no `plugins.*` handle is ever registered.

rows.name: a value that exists ONLY in the legacy project overrides file still reads back after migration
rows.why: The plan's own sharpest warning: `setPluginSetting` has NEVER written to `.omp/plugin-overrides.json`, so for a user who set a project-scope plugin value by hand, that file is the ONLY place the value exists. Drop this read path and every such setting silently reads as its default — data loss with no error, visible only to users who already have a plugin setting configured.
rows.assert: Write `<project>/.omp/plugin-overrides.json` with `settings: { "<plugin>": { <key>: <value> } }`, run the migration, and assert the value is returned by `getPluginSettings` AND that the handle's `provenance(scope)` reports `"project"`.

rows.name: a value that exists ONLY in the legacy runtime config still reads back after migration
rows.assert: Write the legacy `omp-plugins.lock.json` `settings["<plugin>"]["<key>"]`, run the migration, assert the value is returned AND `provenance(scope)` reports `"global"` (it was a global-layer value, so it lands in the global layer of the new shape).

rows.name: the env layer: a declared env var beats a project-layer value and NAMES itself
rows.assert: With the project layer holding a value for the key, set the env var the plugin declared in `definition.env`, and assert BOTH `handle.get(scope)` equals the env-derived value AND `handle.provenance(scope) === "env"`. Per-test `withEnv` with save/restore (copy the helper at `test/config/settings-registry.test.ts:25-37`); do NOT mutate `process.env` at file scope — a full-suite-poisoning env write is a broken test per AGENTS.md.

test_contract.the_trap_in_row_3: `#effectiveEnv` (`config/registry.ts:526-536`) makes env YIELD to a configured layer when the definition sets `envFallback`. The default is `false` (`registry.ts:478` — `typeof env === "object" ? (env.fallback ?? false) : false`), so env wins by default and the row passes. But if the fixture setting declares `envFallback: true`, the env var loses to the project value and `provenance` reports `"project"` — the row would fail, and for CORRECT behaviour. The fixture must NOT declare `envFallback`. The plan never mentions this flag; it is the single easiest way to write a test that is red for the wrong reason and then "fix" it by weakening the assertion.
test_contract.no_mock_module: Never `mock.module()` — it mutates the global module registry and leaks across files. The `PluginManager` rows use per-test `spyOn(piUtils, "getPluginsDir")` / `getPluginsLockfile` / `getProjectDir` / `getProjectPluginOverridesPath` with `mock.restore()` in `afterEach`, exactly as `test/plugin-config.test.ts:25-38` already does. The registry rows use a real `Settings.isolated(...)` instance over a temp dir — no module mocking at all.
test_contract.no_source_grep: The test may assert on the temp config file it wrote (that is behaviour). It may NOT read an implementation `.ts` file and assert on its text — that is banned by AGENTS.md and is not a substitute for any row here.

gate: DONE means all four of: (1) `bun run check:ts` is green; (2) `bun test test/config/plugin-settings-provenance.test.ts` passes all three rows — the two migration rows and the env/provenance row; (3) `bun test test/plugin-config.test.ts test/plugin-config-validate.test.ts test/config/settings-registry.test.ts` is still green; (4) the migration has been manually exercised in the stated order against a real temp project containing a hand-written `.omp/plugin-overrides.json`, and a value deleted from the new store is still gone after a second run (the resurrection check from step 7). Note that (2) cannot be evaluated in this environment until the native addon is built — treat (1) as the only immediately executable gate and (2)-(4) as blocked, not as passing.
gate_can_fail: YES for the type check and the test rows. The provenance row is a real red-to-green: on HEAD there is no `plugins.*` handle to call `provenance()` on at all, so it cannot pass before the work is done. The two migration rows are real red-to-green: on HEAD the new substrate does not exist, and a migration that read only ONE of the two legacy files would leave row 1 or row 2 red. The gate would NOT catch: a migration that runs but re-runs on every start and resurrects deleted keys (only the manual step-7 check in (4) catches that), a wrong-but-plausible env variable name (the row uses whatever name the fixture declares, so a naming slip is invisible to the suite — hence the naming rule must be written down in step 3 and reviewed, not left to the test), and the `deletePluginSetting` semantic change (no row asserts it). Those three are the honest gaps in this gate.
blocks: WI-8b (Option B, `pi.registerSetting`) — explicitly gated on this item. The reason is concrete: 8b's blocker 2 is that a setting id is a bare string with no namespace enforcement, so an extension can collide with a core id, and `register()` throws at `config/registry.ts:787`, breaking at load rather than degrading. The namespace helper built in step 1 IS that enforcement.

WI-11 / WI-12 (M2 wave 8, design-only) — both reason about the second-store problem that this item removes. The plan's own note at line 5994 calls an MCP-contribution design 'exactly the second-store problem that WI-8a Option A exists to solve'.
WI-9 (unload) — indirectly. Only after this item lands is plugin settings state owned by a subsystem with a single substrate that unload can actually clean up.
effort: M (~2-3 days). The plan calls it M with LOW risk; I would raise the risk to MEDIUM and keep M, because the plan under-counts the surface: it names six files and misses `loader.ts:474`, and its risk analysis rests entirely on the provenance test catching the failure, when the more likely failure is the untested resurrection and delete-semantics cases. The typing work (schema→definition adapter, `envFallback` asymmetry, the append-only registry) is more subtle than the plan's 'substrate, not API' framing suggests.
risk: Registering plugin settings dynamically at load time into a registry that has NO unregister (`byId.set` at `config/registry.ts:789` is its only mutation; `resetRegistryForTest` at :953 touches only `effects`). The first load works; the SECOND load of the same plugin in the same process — a reload, a suspend/resume, a second PluginManager in a test file — throws `Setting "plugins.x.y" is registered twice`. That is not a crash in a rare path: suspend/resume is exactly what WI-1 and WI-7 build, and unload is what WI-9 builds, so this item as literally specified would plant a landmine directly in the path of the two items that follow it. The plan's own argument for namespacing is the duplicate throw, and then it specifies a design that walks into it. `registerPluginSetting` returning the existing handle on a repeat lookup is the fix, and it must be step 1, before anything else.
open_questions: `deletePluginSetting` changes meaning. Today it deletes the key outright from the merged store. `handle.unset()` clears the GLOBAL layer only (`unsetGlobalValue`, `config/settings.ts:845`), so a project-layer value correctly resurfaces — that is the right tiering, but it is a behaviour change for `omp plugin config unset` (`cli/plugin-cli.ts:917`). Does 'unset' mean 'forget my global override' (correct tiering, accept the change) or 'remove everywhere' (needs a second project-layer write path)? A human must decide; it is user-visible.

Which Settings layer is the durable home for a plugin setting? The plan says 'overlay' and never names the layer. Global (`handle.set` → `config.yml`) is what the typed core path does and the only one that persists without new machinery, but it puts machine-written third-party keys in a file users hand-edit. The plan itself flags this tension at line 5946 ('Settings is user-edited YAML and is probably the WRONG substrate for internal plugin state'). If the answer is 'not the global layer', this item grows a new store and the whole 'second store' framing changes.

Should the migration marker be a Settings-layer key or a dedicated marker file? A marker file is simpler and cannot be edited away by a user cleaning their config; a Settings key is one less file. Either is defensible — but it must be a deliberate choice, not an accident, because a user who deletes it gets a resurrected-settings bug.

Should a plugin setting be allowed to declare `envFallback`? The naming rule in step 3 covers the opt-IN; it says nothing about the opt-out-that-inverts-priority. Letting a third-party plugin declare `envFallback: true` means its env var yields to a project file, which is probably the opposite of what a plugin author intends.

What happens to `ProjectPluginOverrides.disabled` and `.features`? This item migrates `settings` only. `.omp/plugin-overrides.json` survives with two of its three fields, so the file is NOT removed. Confirm that is intended rather than half-finished.
